definition: In this historical source, novelty refers to the quality of newness that attracts attention and arouses curiosity or interest. It is contrasted with the broader wish to learn simply for information’s sake.

provenance.revision: 1901 New York Macmillan original; archive index checked 2026-10-18
provenance.scope: Source record Curiosity; pinned source text

reasons: The packet does not define novelty as “the quality of newness that attracts attention and arouses curiosity or interest”; it only mentions “interest in novelty” as one of two cases under curiosity.
The contrast in the source is between curiosity/interest in novelty and learning “for the sake of information,” but the definition adds interpretive wording that is not stated in the packet.

The packet distinguishes curiosity from “interest in novelty (Neugier)” and contrasts that with learning “for the sake of information” (Wissbegier), but it does not define novelty as a “quality of newness.”

The packet does not explicitly state that novelty “attracts attention and arouses curiosity or interest”; it only labels one case as “interest in novelty (Neugier)” without describing it in those terms.

Because the central descriptive phrasing about novelty’s effect (“quality of newness,” “attracts attention,” “arouses curiosity”) is not supported by the provided text, the requested sense of the term is not adequately evidenced.
